nodes.title: Arithmetic and Comparison in Expressions
nodes.definition: Polars Expression API supports natural arithmetic and comparison between column expressions. pl.col('a') + pl.col('b') creates a new column expression; comparisons (>, <, ==, !=) return boolean expressions used in filter/when.
key_facts: Arithmetic: pl.col('a') + pl.col('b'), pl.col('x') * 2, pl.col('x') ** 2
Comparisons: pl.col('age') > 30, pl.col('name') == 'Alice'
Logical combinations: & (and), | (or), ~ (not) — use PARENTHESES
Result of arithmetic is an Expr — must be wrapped with .alias() in select/with_columns
Different from pandas: no eval(), no @-references, expressions are lazy

worked_examples.problem: Add two columns into a new 'total' column.
worked_examples.key_insight: Arithmetic between pl.col expressions composes naturally.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use df['a'] + df['b'] — that is pandas series; Polars uses pl.col.
DO NOT use df.eval('a + b') — Polars has no eval method.
Logical: use (cond1) & (cond2), NOT 'and' (Python keyword doesn't work on expressions).

nodes.title: Expression.cast (Type Conversion)
nodes.definition: Expression.cast(dtype, *, strict=True) converts a column expression to a different data type. Common dtypes: pl.Int64, pl.Float64, pl.Utf8 (string), pl.Date, pl.Datetime, pl.Boolean, pl.Categorical.
key_facts: Signature: pl.col(...).cast(pl.Int64) — cast to a Polars dtype
strict=True (default) raises on invalid casts; False returns null
Used inside .with_columns() to modify column type in place
Different from pandas .astype() (which is on Series, not expression)

worked_examples.problem: Cast 'value' column from Float64 to Int64.
solution_steps: Use with_columns to apply the cast
worked_examples.key_insight: cast is an expression method, used inside with_columns.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use .astype() — that is pandas; Polars uses .cast().
Cast inside .select() replaces the column; .with_columns() keeps others.

nodes.title: LazyFrame.collect (Trigger Execution)
nodes.definition: LazyFrame.collect(*, engine='auto'|'streaming'|'in-memory') executes the query plan and returns a DataFrame. In Polars 1.0+, engine='streaming' enables out-of-core execution for results larger than RAM.
key_facts: Method on LazyFrame, returns DataFrame
engine='streaming' in 1.0+ replaces older streaming=True parameter
Without .collect() lazy operations do not execute

worked_examples.problem: Collect a LazyFrame with default in-memory engine.
solution_steps: Build LazyFrame via scan_csv / LazyFrame / df.lazy()
worked_examples.key_insight: collect() materializes the query plan into a DataFrame.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT pass `streaming=True` to .collect() in Polars 1.0+; use engine='streaming'.
Calling .collect() in a loop defeats lazy optimization.

nodes.title: Complex Types: List, Struct, Categorical Namespaces
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ supports complex column types: List (array per row), Struct (named fields per row), Categorical (memory-efficient string). Each has its own namespace for operations: list.eval, list.len, struct.field, and Categorical via cast(pl.Categorical).
key_facts: List ops: pl.col(x).list.eval(expr), .list.len(), .list.contains(val), .explode()
list.eval uses pl.element() to reference each list element inside the expr
Struct: pl.col(x).struct.field('name'), pl.col(x).struct.rename_fields(...)
Categorical: pl.col(x).cast(pl.Categorical) — memory-efficient string repr
Categorical has .cat namespace: .cat.get_categories(), .cat.set_ordering()

worked_examples.problem: Double each element inside a list column.
solution_steps: Inside list.eval, pl.element() references each list element
worked_examples.key_insight: list.eval + pl.element() is the canonical way to map over list contents.

worked_examples.problem: Extract field 'x' from struct column 'data'.
worked_examples.key_insight: struct.field is the safe way to access struct fields (vs dict indexing).

worked_examples.problem: Cast string column to Categorical for memory savings.
worked_examples.key_insight: Categorical dtype uses dictionary encoding; ideal for repeated strings.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use map_elements / apply over lists — use list.eval instead (faster).
DO NOT access struct fields with bracket [] — Polars uses .struct.field('name').
DO NOT use astype('category') — pandas style; Polars uses cast(pl.Categorical).

nodes.title: Cumulative Operations (cum_sum, cum_max, cum_min, cum_prod) — Polars 1.0+ Names
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ renamed cumulative methods to snake_case: cum_sum, cum_max, cum_min, cum_prod, cum_count. Polars 0.x used cumsum, cummax (no underscore). These compute running aggregates over a column.
key_facts: Polars 1.0+: cum_sum, cum_max, cum_min, cum_prod, cum_count (snake_case)
Polars 0.x (deprecated): cumsum, cummax, cummin (no underscore)
.cum_sum() returns expression of same length with running totals
Can combine with .over('group') for per-group cumulative
reverse=True parameter computes cumulative from end to start

worked_examples.problem: Compute cumulative sum of column 'x'.
worked_examples.key_insight: cum_sum is the Polars 1.0+ canonical name; older cumsum is deprecated.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use .cumsum() — that is the deprecated Polars 0.x name.
DO NOT use np.cumsum() — Polars expressions are independent.
DO NOT use pandas .cumsum() — Polars uses cum_sum (with underscore).

nodes.title: Datetime Namespace (pl.col.dt.*)
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ provides date/datetime operations via the `.dt` namespace: extract components (year, month, day, hour, etc.), truncate to time unit, offset by duration string, convert timezone, format as string.
key_facts: pl.col('ts').dt.year() / .month() / .day() / .hour() / .minute() — components (Int)
pl.col('ts').dt.truncate('1mo') — round DOWN to time unit (e.g., '1mo', '1d', '1h')
pl.col('ts').dt.offset_by('1d') — add a duration
pl.col('ts').dt.weekday() — day of week (1-7 in Polars 1.0+, was 0-6 in 0.x)
Duration strings: 'ns', 'us', 'ms', 's', 'm', 'h', 'd', 'w', 'mo', 'q', 'y'

worked_examples.problem: Extract year and month from timestamp.
worked_examples.key_insight: dt namespace extracts components without manual datetime parsing.

worked_examples.problem: Truncate timestamp to start of month.
worked_examples.key_insight: truncate rounds DOWN to the time unit boundary.

worked_examples.problem: Add 1 day to a timestamp.
worked_examples.key_insight: offset_by adds a duration string — clean alternative to manual timedelta.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use pd.DatetimeIndex / pd.to_datetime — Polars has native datetime ops.
DO NOT use ts + timedelta(days=1) — Polars uses dt.offset_by('1d').
DO NOT use .dt.floor() — Polars uses .dt.truncate() for the same effect.
Polars weekday is 1-indexed in 1.0+ (Monday=1); was 0-indexed in 0.x.

nodes.title: group_by_dynamic Advanced Parameters (period, offset, closed)
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ group_by_dynamic supports advanced time-window parameters beyond `every`: `period` controls window length (default = every), `offset` shifts window boundaries, `closed` controls boundary inclusivity. These enable overlapping or shifted time windows.
key_facts: every: stride between window starts (e.g., '1d')
period: window length (default = every; period > every creates overlapping)
offset: shift window start (e.g., '12h' for half-day-shifted bins)
closed: 'left' (default), 'right', 'both', 'none' — boundary inclusion
Index column MUST be sorted; use df.sort('ts') first

worked_examples.problem: Overlapping 2-day windows every 1 day (rolling daily).
worked_examples.key_insight: every < period creates overlapping windows for rolling-style time aggregation.

worked_examples.problem: Bins offset by 12 hours (custom day boundary).
solution_steps: Bins now start at noon, not midnight
worked_examples.key_insight: offset shifts bin boundaries — useful for business-day boundaries.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use groupby_dynamic — that's deprecated 0.x; use group_by_dynamic.
Failing to sort by index column produces incorrect grouping silently.
period < every creates GAPS in coverage (some rows skipped).
DO NOT use pandas resample/rolling — Polars has its own time-aware grouping.

nodes.title: Polars Expression API (pl.col, alias, etc.)
nodes.definition: Polars expressions are composable, lazy descriptions of column-level computations. pl.col('name') references a column; chained methods like .mean(), .alias('new_name') build the expression. Used with .select(), .with_columns(), .filter(), .group_by().agg().
key_facts: pl.col(column_name) creates a column expression
.alias('new_name') renames the resulting column
.mean(), .sum(), .min(), .max(), .std(), .var() are aggregations
Arithmetic: pl.col('a') + pl.col('b'), pl.col('x') * 2
Comparison returns boolean expression: pl.col('age') > 30

worked_examples.problem: Compute mean of 'price' column with alias 'avg_price'.
solution_steps: Use pl.col('price') to reference the column
worked_examples.key_insight: Expressions compose: column ref → operation → alias → context.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use pandas-style df['price'].mean() — Polars expressions are lazy.
DO NOT call .expr() — that method does not exist; expressions are created by pl.col() directly.
DO NOT call .to_scalar() on an aggregation — wrap in pl.DataFrame or use .select() which returns a 1-row DataFrame.
Expression must be used inside a context: select / with_columns / filter / group_by.agg.

nodes.title: DataFrame.filter (Row Filtering)
nodes.definition: DataFrame.filter(predicate) returns rows where the boolean expression evaluates to True. The predicate is a Polars expression (typically comparison or logical combination).
key_facts: Signature: df.filter(pl.col('age') > 30)
Combine with & (and), | (or), ~ (not): df.filter((pl.col('a') > 0) & (pl.col('b') < 10))
Works on both DataFrame and LazyFrame
Different from pandas df[df['x'] > 0]: polars uses .filter() method

worked_examples.problem: Filter rows where age > 30.
worked_examples.key_insight: filter() takes a polars expression, not pandas boolean mask.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use df[df['x'] > 0] — that is pandas; Polars uses df.filter().
Combining conditions: use & / | with parentheses, NOT 'and' / 'or'.

nodes.title: Conditional Aggregation via Expression.filter()
nodes.definition: Polars supports conditional aggregation by chaining .filter(predicate) INSIDE an expression before the aggregation. This is different from DataFrame.filter() (row filter). Inside an expression, .filter() applies BEFORE the aggregation, so SUM/MEAN apply only to values where the predicate is true.
key_facts: Syntax: pl.col('y').filter(pl.col('x') > 2).sum() — sum y where x > 2
Different from df.filter() (row-level): expression .filter() is conditional aggregation
Useful for computing 'sum of x where y > 0' without modifying input DataFrame
Can be combined: pl.col('y').filter(condition).mean().alias('cond_mean')
Pandas equivalent would be df[cond]['y'].sum() — Polars version is cleaner

worked_examples.problem: Sum 'y' but only for rows where 'x' > 2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Filter inside expression = conditional aggregation, no need to pre-filter DataFrame.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT confuse Expression.filter() (conditional agg) with DataFrame.filter() (row filter).
DO NOT use df.query('x > 2')['y'].sum() — pandas style.
DO NOT do df.filter(cond).select(pl.col('y').sum()) — works but wastes a step.

nodes.title: DataFrame.group_by (Aggregation)
nodes.definition: DataFrame.group_by(*by, *, maintain_order=False).agg(*exprs) groups rows by one or more columns and applies aggregation expressions. Returns a new DataFrame with one row per group. Note: Polars 1.0+ uses `group_by` (with underscore), NOT `groupby` (pandas style).
key_facts: Signature: df.group_by('col').agg(pl.col('x').sum().alias('total'))
Polars 1.0+ method name is group_by (snake_case with underscore)
Polars 0.x used .groupby() — renamed in 1.0
Pass multiple columns: df.group_by('a', 'b').agg(...)
Aggregations: .sum(), .mean(), .first(), .last(), .count(), .min(), .max()

worked_examples.problem: Group by 'group', sum 'value' as 'total'.
worked_examples.key_insight: group_by + agg is the standard aggregation pattern.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use df.groupby() (without underscore) — that is pandas/old Polars.
DO NOT forget .alias() — default name is the input column.

nodes.title: DataFrame.group_by_dynamic (Time-Based Grouping)
nodes.definition: DataFrame.group_by_dynamic(index_column, *, every, period=None, offset=None, closed='left', ...).agg(...) groups rows into time-based windows. The method name was RENAMED from groupby_dynamic in Polars 0.x to group_by_dynamic in Polars 1.0+.
key_facts: Signature: df.group_by_dynamic('timestamp', every='1d').agg(...)
Polars 1.0+ method name is `group_by_dynamic` (was `groupby_dynamic` in 0.x)
every parameter: window size, e.g. '1d', '1h', '30m', '1mo'
period parameter: optional, lookback window if different from every
offset parameter: optional, shift window boundaries
The index column must be sorted by time (use df.sort('ts') first)

worked_examples.problem: Group hourly data into daily buckets, sum 'value' per day.
solution_steps: Sort df by timestamp first (required for dynamic grouping)
worked_examples.key_insight: group_by_dynamic + every is the canonical Polars 1.0+ time-bucketing pattern.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use .groupby_dynamic() — that is the deprecated 0.x name.
DO NOT use .groupby_rolling() — that is also a deprecated 0.x name; Polars 1.0+ uses .rolling() (different semantics) or group_by_dynamic.
DO NOT use pandas .resample() — that is pandas API.
Unsorted timestamp column causes incorrect grouping; sort first.

nodes.title: DataFrame.join
nodes.definition: DataFrame.join(other, on=None, *, how='inner', left_on=None, right_on=None, suffix='_right', validate=None) joins two DataFrames on key column(s). Supports multiple join strategies and optional validation of cardinality.
key_facts: Signature: df_a.join(df_b, on='id', how='left'/'inner'/'outer'/'cross', ...)
on parameter for single key; left_on / right_on for different key names
how parameter: 'inner' (default), 'left', 'outer', 'cross', 'semi', 'anti'
suffix parameter to disambiguate duplicate columns (default '_right')
validate parameter (Polars 1.0+) for cardinality assertion

worked_examples.problem: Left join df_a and df_b on 'id' with 1:1 validation.
solution_steps: Add validate='1:1' to enforce one-to-one mapping
worked_examples.key_insight: Polars 1.0+ join with validate ensures cardinality at join time.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use pd.merge — that is pandas; use df.join.
Default how is 'inner' — explicitly specify 'left' when needed.

nodes.title: df.join_asof (As-Of / Temporal Join)
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ df.join_asof is a time-series 'as-of' join: for each row in the left DataFrame, finds the MOST RECENT matching row in the right DataFrame at or before (or after) that row's index value. Used for trades-quotes matching, sensor-timestamp alignment, etc.
key_facts: Signature: df_a.join_asof(df_b, on='time_col', strategy='backward')
strategy: 'backward' (most recent <=), 'forward' (next >=), 'nearest'
BOTH DataFrames must be SORTED by the asof column
tolerance parameter: max time delta (returns null if exceeded)
by parameter: additional exact-match columns (e.g., per-symbol)

worked_examples.problem: Match trades to most recent quote (backward asof).
worked_examples.key_insight: join_asof is essential for time-series alignment problems.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use pd.merge_asof — Polars has native join_asof.
Failing to sort both DataFrames by the asof column gives wrong results.
Default strategy is 'backward' — be explicit when needing 'forward' or 'nearest'.

nodes.title: Join Strategies (anti, semi, outer) + left_on/right_on
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ supports rich join strategies via the `how` parameter: 'inner' (default), 'left', 'outer'/'full', 'cross', 'semi' (rows in A also in B), 'anti' (rows in A NOT in B). The left_on/right_on parameters allow joining DataFrames with DIFFERENT key column names.
key_facts: how options: 'inner', 'left', 'outer'/'full', 'cross', 'semi', 'anti'
'anti' join: rows in left WITHOUT matching key in right (set difference)
'semi' join: rows in left WITH matching key (set intersection on keys only)
left_on / right_on: join on differently-named columns
Anti/semi joins do NOT bring right-side columns (only left)

worked_examples.problem: Anti join to find rows in df_a NOT in df_b.
solution_steps: Result has only df_a's columns; only rows missing from df_b
worked_examples.key_insight: Anti join replaces complex 'not in' filters.

worked_examples.problem: Join with differently-named key columns.
worked_examples.key_insight: left_on/right_on enable joins without renaming columns first.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use ~df['id'].isin(df_b['id']) for anti join — Polars has how='anti'.
DO NOT use pd.merge with indicator parameter — Polars uses 'anti'/'semi'.
Forgetting 'how' parameter defaults to 'inner' — be explicit.

nodes.title: Lag / Lead Operations (diff, shift)
nodes.definition: Polars provides lag/lead via .diff() (current - previous) and .shift(n) (returns values from n rows back). Both produce a column with the same length, with leading nulls equal to abs(n).
key_facts: pl.col(x).diff() — equivalent to pl.col(x) - pl.col(x).shift(1)
pl.col(x).shift(1) — value from previous row (lag-1)
pl.col(x).shift(-1) — value from next row (lead-1)
First abs(n) values are null (no prior/next row exists)
Output dtype: same as input (or Int64 for diff on int)

worked_examples.problem: Add 'diff' column (current - previous) using diff().
worked_examples.key_insight: diff() is shorthand for shift(1) subtraction.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use df['x'].diff() — pandas style; Polars uses pl.col expression.
DO NOT manually compute pl.col('x') - pl.col('x').shift(1) when .diff() suffices.
First row will be null after diff — don't forget to fill_null if needed.

nodes.title: Lazy Query Optimization (explain, eager_to_lazy, predicate pushdown)
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ LazyFrame provides query plan introspection and optimization. lf.explain() returns a textual query plan showing optimizations like predicate pushdown and projection pushdown. df.lazy() converts eager DataFrame to LazyFrame for further lazy chaining.
key_facts: lf.explain() — returns query plan as string (shows pushdowns, optimizations)
df.lazy() — convert eager DataFrame to LazyFrame (for lazy chaining)
Predicate pushdown: filters move closer to scan (skip rows during IO)
Projection pushdown: only required columns are read
lf.show_graph() — visualize plan (requires graphviz)

worked_examples.problem: Inspect query plan with explain.
worked_examples.key_insight: explain() shows you what optimizations Polars will apply at collect time.

worked_examples.problem: Convert eager DataFrame to LazyFrame.
solution_steps: Call df.lazy() to get a LazyFrame
worked_examples.key_insight: df.lazy() is the bridge from eager to lazy execution.

worked_examples.problem: Chained lazy operations.
solution_steps: Multiple lazy ops can be chained before collect
Polars optimizes the whole plan together
worked_examples.key_insight: Chained lazy ops let Polars optimize across the whole pipeline.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT call .collect() between every operation — defeats lazy optimization.
DO NOT use pl.LazyFrame(df) — use df.lazy() (cleaner).
lf.explain() returns a string, not a DataFrame — print it to read.

nodes.title: Polars LazyFrame and Lazy Execution
nodes.definition: A LazyFrame is Polars' deferred-execution counterpart to DataFrame. Operations on a LazyFrame build a query plan that is only executed when .collect() is called. This enables query optimization (predicate pushdown, projection pushdown) and out-of-memory streaming.
key_facts: Create via pl.LazyFrame({...}) or pl.scan_*() functions
Operations like .filter, .select, .with_columns return a new LazyFrame
Execution is triggered by .collect() or .sink_*() methods
Polars 1.0+ provides explicit streaming engine via engine='streaming'
Eager DataFrame can be converted to LazyFrame via df.lazy()

worked_examples.problem: Read CSV lazily, filter age > 30, then collect.
solution_steps: Use pl.scan_csv() to create a LazyFrame from CSV
Apply .filter(pl.col('age') > 30) — still lazy, no IO yet
Call .collect() to execute the query and get a DataFrame
worked_examples.key_insight: Lazy operations defer execution; collect() materializes the result.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT pass `lazy=True` to pl.read_csv — that parameter does not exist. Use pl.scan_csv() instead.
Calling .collect() on every operation defeats the purpose of lazy execution.
Polars 0.x methods like df.lazy().with_column() are renamed in 1.0+

nodes.title: Null Handling Expressions (fill_null, is_null, is_not_null, drop_nulls)
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ provides comprehensive null handling via expressions: fill_null(value) replaces nulls with a value; is_null() / is_not_null() are boolean predicates; drop_nulls() removes rows with any null.
key_facts: pl.col(x).fill_null(value) — replace nulls with constant value or expression
pl.col(x).is_null() — returns boolean Series (True where null)
pl.col(x).is_not_null() — inverse of is_null()
df.drop_nulls() — remove rows with null in any column
df.drop_nulls(subset=['x']) — only check specific columns

worked_examples.problem: Fill null values in column 'x' with 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: fill_null is the Polars equivalent of pandas fillna.

worked_examples.problem: Filter rows where column 'x' is not null.
worked_examples.key_insight: is_not_null + filter is more explicit than dropna.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use pandas-style df['x'].fillna(0) — Polars uses expressions.
DO NOT use .dropna() — Polars uses .drop_nulls().
DO NOT use .isnull() / .notna() — Polars uses .is_null() / .is_not_null().

nodes.title: Reshape Operations: pivot, unpivot, explode, concat strategies
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ provides DataFrame reshape ops: pivot (long→wide), unpivot (wide→long, renamed from .melt in 0.x), explode (list cells → rows), and pl.concat with strategies ('vertical', 'vertical_relaxed', 'diagonal', 'diagonal_relaxed', 'horizontal') for combining DataFrames.
key_facts: df.pivot(index, on, values) — Polars 1.0+ uses `on=` (not `columns=` from 0.x)
df.unpivot(index, on) — Polars 1.0+ name (was df.melt in 0.x)
df.explode('list_col') — one row per list element
pl.concat(dfs, how='vertical') — stack with same schema (strict)
pl.concat(dfs, how='vertical_relaxed') — auto coerce dtypes
pl.concat(dfs, how='diagonal_relaxed') — different cols, fill nulls + coerce

worked_examples.problem: Pivot DataFrame from long to wide.
worked_examples.key_insight: Pivot uses `on=` for the column-pivoting parameter (1.0+ name).

worked_examples.problem: Unpivot wide DataFrame to long.
worked_examples.key_insight: unpivot is the Polars 1.0+ name for what pandas calls melt.

worked_examples.problem: Concat with type coercion.
solution_steps: df1 has int b; df2 has float b — incompatible for strict vertical
Use pl.concat([df1, df2], how='vertical_relaxed') to auto-coerce
worked_examples.key_insight: Use *_relaxed strategies when DataFrames have compatible-but-different dtypes.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use df.pivot(columns='b') — that's the 0.x parameter name; use `on=`.
DO NOT use df.melt() — Polars 1.0+ uses df.unpivot().
DO NOT use pd.concat — Polars uses pl.concat.
Strict 'vertical' concat fails with dtype mismatch — use *_relaxed.

nodes.title: df.rolling (Time-Aware Rolling Windows)
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ df.rolling(index_column, period) provides time-aware rolling windows. Unlike group_by_dynamic (which produces NEW rows), rolling preserves the original row count and adds a rolling window aggregate per row. Polars 0.x called this groupby_rolling (deprecated).
key_facts: Polars 1.0+: df.rolling(index_column='ts', period='2d')
Polars 0.x (deprecated): df.groupby_rolling(...)
index_column must be sorted (typically datetime or numeric)
period is the LOOKBACK window (e.g., '7d' = past 7 days)
Output has same row count as input (per-row aggregation)

worked_examples.problem: Rolling sum of past 2 days for each row.
worked_examples.key_insight: df.rolling = time-aware rolling; row count preserved.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use groupby_rolling — that's deprecated 0.x.
DO NOT use pandas df.rolling().sum() — different semantics (fixed-size).
Polars rolling is TIME-aware (period like '2d'); pandas is COUNT-based.
Index column must be SORTED, otherwise results are incorrect.

nodes.title: pl.scan_csv (Lazy CSV Reading)
nodes.definition: pl.scan_csv(source, *, has_header=True, separator=',', schema=None, ...) creates a LazyFrame from one or more CSV files without loading data into memory. Predicate and projection pushdown are applied during .collect().
key_facts: Signature: pl.scan_csv(source: str | Path | list[str | Path], ...) -> LazyFrame
Returns LazyFrame (not DataFrame). Pair with .collect() to materialize.
Supports glob patterns: pl.scan_csv('data/*.csv')
schema parameter (dict) for explicit dtype hints
Eager alternative is pl.read_csv() which loads into memory immediately

worked_examples.problem: Lazily scan a CSV, filter rows, and collect.
solution_steps: Call pl.scan_csv with the file path
Call .collect() to execute and return a DataFrame
worked_examples.key_insight: scan_csv defers IO; predicate pushdown skips rows without reading them.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT write pl.read_csv(path, lazy=True) — read_csv has no lazy parameter.
DO NOT use pd.read_csv from pandas; use polars' own scan_csv.
Forgetting .collect() returns a LazyFrame, not data.

nodes.title: pl.scan_csv Advanced Usage (schema, glob, n_rows)
nodes.definition: Beyond basic lazy CSV reading, pl.scan_csv supports advanced parameters: explicit `schema` dict for dtype control (avoids inference cost and ensures correctness), GLOB patterns for multiple files (e.g., 'data/*.csv'), and `n_rows` to limit rows for development/testing.
key_facts: schema parameter: dict[str, pl.DataType] for explicit dtype hints
Glob patterns work natively: pl.scan_csv('dir/*.csv')
n_rows: limit rows scanned (useful for sampling)
schema dict avoids dtype inference (faster, deterministic)
Glob auto-concatenates results from all matching files

worked_examples.problem: Scan CSV with explicit schema and glob.
solution_steps: Pass schema={'name': pl.Utf8, 'age': pl.Int64} to scan_csv
worked_examples.key_insight: Schema + glob make scan_csv production-ready for typed multi-file pipelines.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use `dtype=` parameter — it doesn't exist; use `schema=` dict.
DO NOT manually loop with glob.glob() + concat; pl.scan_csv accepts globs directly.
schema dict must include ALL columns, not just some (or use `schema_overrides`).

nodes.title: pl.scan_ndjson (Lazy JSON Lines Reading)
nodes.definition: pl.scan_ndjson(source) lazily reads newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON / JSON Lines) files where each line is a separate JSON object. This is the common format for log files, event streams, and big-data exports. Different from pl.read_json (which reads a single JSON array).
key_facts: Signature: pl.scan_ndjson(source: str | Path | list) -> LazyFrame
Each line in source file must be a complete JSON object
Auto-infers schema from first rows
Eager alternative: pl.read_ndjson
Different from pl.read_json (JSON array format)

worked_examples.problem: Lazily scan JSON Lines file.
solution_steps: Call pl.scan_ndjson with the .ndjson or .jsonl file path
worked_examples.key_insight: scan_ndjson is the streaming counterpart for JSON Lines / NDJSON format.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use pl.read_json — that is for JSON arrays, not NDJSON.
DO NOT use pl.scan_json (doesn't exist) — only pl.scan_ndjson.
DO NOT manually json.loads each line; pl.scan_ndjson handles it.

nodes.title: pl.scan_parquet (Lazy Parquet Reading)
nodes.definition: pl.scan_parquet(source, *, n_rows=None, ...) creates a LazyFrame from Parquet file(s) without loading data. Supports column pruning and row-group level filtering via predicate pushdown.
key_facts: Signature: pl.scan_parquet(source: str | Path | list, ...) -> LazyFrame
Use .select('col1', 'col2') to leverage column projection pushdown
Eager alternative is pl.read_parquet()
Supports multiple files: pl.scan_parquet(['a.parquet', 'b.parquet'])

worked_examples.problem: Lazily scan parquet, select only 'name' column.
solution_steps: Call pl.scan_parquet with the file path
Chain .select('name') — only this column will be read
worked_examples.key_insight: scan_parquet + select uses projection pushdown — IO skips other columns.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use pl.read_parquet for lazy reads.
Without .select() projection pushdown does not occur.

nodes.title: lf.sink_parquet (Streaming Parquet Write)
nodes.definition: LazyFrame.sink_parquet(path, *, compression='zstd', statistics=True, engine='streaming') writes a LazyFrame to a Parquet file in streaming mode without materializing the full result in memory. This is the Polars 1.0+ way to handle datasets larger than RAM.
key_facts: Signature: lf.sink_parquet(path, *, statistics=True/False/'full', ...)
Operates on LazyFrame (lf), NOT eager DataFrame (df)
statistics parameter accepts True / False / 'full' / 'minimal' (1.0+)
Returns None (writes to disk as side effect)
Polars 1.0+ alternative: .collect(engine='streaming') (for in-memory result)
Eager DataFrame uses df.write_parquet() (DOES load into memory)

worked_examples.problem: Stream a LazyFrame to parquet with full statistics.
solution_steps: Start with a LazyFrame `lf` (from scan_csv, LazyFrame constructor, etc.)
No need to call .collect() — sink does streaming write internally
worked_examples.key_insight: sink_parquet is the streaming write counterpart of scan_parquet.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT write `df.write_parquet(path, streaming=True)` — there is no such parameter on write_parquet (which is eager).
DO NOT call .collect() before .sink_parquet() — this defeats streaming.
sink_parquet is on LazyFrame; write_parquet is on DataFrame — they are NOT interchangeable.
DO NOT use df.to_parquet() — that is pandas API.

nodes.title: Polars 1.0+ Streaming I/O (sink_csv, collect engine='streaming')
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ provides streaming execution for both writing (sink_csv, sink_parquet) and collecting larger-than-memory queries via engine='streaming'. The old Polars 0.x `streaming=True` parameter is replaced by `engine='streaming'`.
key_facts: lf.sink_csv(path) writes LazyFrame to CSV in streaming mode
lf.collect(engine='streaming') runs the query out-of-core
Polars 1.0+ API: `engine='streaming'`, NOT `streaming=True` (0.x deprecated)
Streaming execution processes chunks instead of full materialization
Available engines: 'auto' (default), 'streaming', 'in-memory'

worked_examples.problem: Stream a LazyFrame to CSV (no memory load).
worked_examples.key_insight: sink_csv is the streaming CSV counterpart of sink_parquet.

worked_examples.problem: Collect a LazyFrame using streaming engine.
worked_examples.key_insight: engine='streaming' replaces the deprecated streaming=True parameter.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use `streaming=True` to collect() — that's the deprecated 0.x API.
DO NOT use df.write_csv() with `streaming=True` — that parameter doesn't exist.
Use lf.sink_csv() (LazyFrame method), not df.write_csv() (eager DataFrame).

nodes.title: String Namespace (pl.col.str.*)
nodes.definition: Polars 1.0+ provides string operations via the `.str` namespace on column expressions: contains (regex/literal), split, len_chars/len_bytes, replace, to_lowercase/to_uppercase, slice, strip, and more.
key_facts: pl.col('s').str.contains(pattern) — regex by default; literal=True for literal match
pl.col('s').str.split(separator) — returns List[Utf8]
pl.col('s').str.len_chars() / .len_bytes() — character/byte count
pl.col('s').str.replace(pat, repl) — first occurrence replace
pl.col('s').str.to_lowercase() / .to_uppercase() — case conversion

worked_examples.problem: Add boolean 'has_a' column where 'name' starts with 'A'.
worked_examples.key_insight: str namespace methods chain naturally with other expression ops.

worked_examples.problem: Count words by splitting on space.
solution_steps: Use pl.col('text').str.split(' ').list.len() to count list items
worked_examples.key_insight: str.split + list.len combines namespaces for word counting.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use df['s'].str.contains() — pandas style; Polars uses pl.col.
DO NOT use .str.len() — ambiguous; use .str.len_chars() or .str.len_bytes().
Default contains uses REGEX; use literal=True for literal substring match.

nodes.title: Join validate Parameter (Polars 1.0+ Strict '1:1' Format)
nodes.definition: The validate parameter on .join() enforces cardinality constraints at join time. In Polars 1.0+, the canonical accepted values use the STRICT FORMAT '1:1', '1:m', 'm:1', 'm:m' (with a colon separator). These are different from pandas' 'one_to_one' / 'one_to_many' format.
key_facts: Polars 1.0+ canonical format: '1:1', '1:m', 'm:1', 'm:m' (colon)
Pandas uses 'one_to_one', 'one_to_many', etc. — DIFFERENT format
If validation fails, Polars raises ComputeError
validate=None (default) means no validation

worked_examples.problem: Enforce 1-to-1 join validation on df_a and df_b.
solution_steps: Add validate='1:1' to .join() call (note: COLON, NOT hyphen/underscore)
Raises if either side has duplicate keys
worked_examples.key_insight: Polars 1.0+ uses '1:1' format; pandas-style 'one_to_one' is NOT canonical here.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT write validate='one_to_one' — that is pandas format.
DO NOT write validate='one-to-one' — also not canonical Polars 1.0+.
DO NOT write validate='1-1' — must use COLON '1:1'.
The exact 3-character string '1:1' is the Polars 1.0+ standard.

nodes.title: pl.when / .then / .otherwise (Conditional Expressions)
nodes.definition: pl.when(condition).then(value_if_true).otherwise(value_if_false) builds a conditional expression for row-wise branching. Used inside .select() or .with_columns() to create derived columns.
key_facts: Signature: pl.when(cond).then(expr).otherwise(expr)
Can chain multiple: pl.when(c1).then(v1).when(c2).then(v2).otherwise(v3)
Wrap literal values with pl.lit() for clarity
Add .alias('col_name') at the end to name the result

worked_examples.problem: Add a 'category' column: 'young' if age <= 30, else 'old'.
worked_examples.key_insight: when/then/otherwise is Polars' equivalent of np.where / pandas .apply.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use np.where() — that is numpy; use pl.when().then().otherwise().
DO NOT use df.apply() — slow and pandas-style; use Polars expressions.
Forgetting .alias() leaves a default unnamed column.

nodes.title: Expression.over (Window Functions)
nodes.definition: Expression.over(*group_cols) is Polars' window function: it computes an aggregation WITHIN each group but keeps the original row count (unlike group_by().agg() which collapses rows).
key_facts: Signature: pl.col('x').mean().over('group') — mean of x per group
Each row keeps its own value but shows the group-level aggregation
Used inside .with_columns() or .select()
Different from .group_by('group').agg(...) which reduces row count

worked_examples.problem: Compute per-group mean of 'value', keeping original rows.
solution_steps: Use with_columns to add as new column
worked_examples.key_insight: over() is the SQL window function equivalent in Polars.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use df.groupby('group')['value'].transform('mean') — pandas style.
DO NOT use .group_by().agg() for window — that reduces rows.

nodes.title: DataFrame.with_columns (Add or Modify Columns)
nodes.definition: DataFrame.with_columns(*exprs, **named_exprs) returns a new DataFrame with one or more added or replaced columns. Each expression must produce a column (e.g., pl.col(...).some_op().alias('new_name')).
key_facts: Signature: df.with_columns(*exprs) -> DataFrame
Accepts multiple expressions: df.with_columns(expr1, expr2)
Replaces a column if the alias matches an existing name
Preserves all other columns (vs .select which keeps only selected)

worked_examples.problem: Add a 'doubled' column to df.
worked_examples.key_insight: with_columns is the canonical way to add/modify columns.

common_pitfalls: DO NOT use df['new'] = ... — Polars DataFrames are immutable.
Forgetting .alias() means the new column overrides the source column.
